claims.text: Nanoscale layering creates closely spaced interlayer interfaces in high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Closely spaced interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion and slower diffusion reduce elevated-temperature time-dependent plastic flow.
The proposed coatings can be refractory-HEA or CoCrFeNi-based nanoscale multilayers with coherent, stable interfaces.
Changing the multilayer period from approximately 20 to 200 nm changes the spacing of interlayer boundaries.
High-temperature nanoindentation can be used to measure time-dependent deformation in HEAs.
The relevant creep response can be tested at 600–800 °C under constant stress or stress relaxation in vacuum or inert gas.
Nanoscale boundaries between compositionally different HEA layers are the structural mediator governing creep resistance.
Interfaces block or slow dislocation glide and climb.
Multi-element site distortions reduce diffusion rates.
Interfacial obstruction of dislocations and reduced diffusion collectively enhance high-temperature creep resistance.
Thinner, stable multilayers will have lower creep strain rates than a monolithic HEA coating with the same overall composition and thickness.
Thinner, stable multilayers will have higher creep stress exponents than the monolithic baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the multilayer interfaces remain stable and do not undergo interfacial phase transformations.
The proposed mechanism remains applicable up to approximately 800 °C.
The dominant interfacial process may be interface sliding or dislocation pile-up and may vary with composition and layer thickness.

Failure to observe either a creep-rate difference, altered dislocation-interface interactions, or reduced dislocation mobility in multilayers relative to the single-layer control would falsify the hypothesis.
